In the days after the accident, not in their wildest nightmares had anyone guessed, they would soon be eating each other. So those who died in the crash had been buried haphazardly around the plane. But the avalanche had dumped a few extra meters of snow across the entire valley, and nobody was sure where the graves had been. Finding these bodies in particular was especially important for a somewhat gory reason. The unfortunate souls who died in the crash would have been healthy right up to the last second. That meant their bodies would provide significantly more meat. So, how do you find a dead body under several meters of snow when you don't have any tools and you aren't sure where to dig? As always, the endlessly inventive survivors came up with a creative solution. They dug narrow prospecting shafts in the snow by weeing in the same spot until they hit either a body or the solid ice of the glacia. But as the rations began to dwindle, they were forced to be significantly less picky. They ate internal organs and the meager scraps of flesh scraped from hands and feet. They squeezed the gunk out of intestines and sliced up what was left. They cracked bones to get at the marrow. They even ate the brains. By this point, cannibalism had become so common place that survivors started using human bones as utensils. A few even repurposed halved skulls as bowls for the brewing of broths and soups. You're probably starting to get a sense of how that first picture came to be. At first, it's hard to get your head around a group of boys smiling beside the spinal column of one of their friends. But by then they knew their friends were gone. What was left was just food. Not everyone was able to stomach it. Numa Tokati in particular never quite got over his revulsion. When he'd been on the expedition team, he'd managed to force down his meat ration for the good of the group. He knew he'd need all the strength he could get to make it out of the mountains and fetch help. But now with his injury continuing to trouble him, he refused to eat anything at all. And with every day passing, he was getting weaker. Down at the tail, things were equally desperate, though for different reasons. Despite several days of solid work on the radio, Roy Harley had made the sum total of no progress whatsoever. He had no way of knowing it, but the truth is he was wasting his time. The Fairchild radio ran on 115V AC power, but the batteries were only able to supply 24V DC power. Roy had been destined to fail from the very start. After eight fruitless and frustrating days, he finally gave up and Operation Radio for Help was officially mothballled. But it hadn't been a complete failure. During the week or so they'd spent living in the tail cone, the expedition team had had plenty of time to poke around a bit, and Tintin had made a discovery that would ultimately change the course of this entire story. The tail contains the Fairchild's heating system. Now, a little bit of central heating would have been lovely, but just like the radio, unpowered, the heating system was useless. But it wasn't the system itself that interested Tintin. It was the copious quantity of insulation it was wrapped in. Thin, strong, and light. It had given him an idea. The biggest challenge they'd faced so far on every single expedition was how to navigate the nights. The days were brutally hard, but just about doable. The nights, they were completely deadly. If they were ever going to escape the mountains, they needed a more reliable way of surviving when the sun went down. And that's where the heating insulation came in. Using more copper wire salvaged from the cockpit as Fred, the survivors began painstakingly stitching the insulation into a giant sack just big enough for free people to huddle inside. In what was proving to be the hardest survival RPG ever conceived, this crude sleeping bag was the last piece of gear they needed to face the final boss. With it, they were ready for one last assault on the mountains. It was time to get the hell out of there. Drawing on all their experience from the previous expeditions, they prepared everything down to the smallest detail. They built up a healthy stockpile of freshly cut meat from newly found bodies and packed the warmest clothes and plenty of spare blankets into improvised napsacks. Sunburn was starting to become a real issue during the day, so the survivors used makeup salvaged from the dead to protect their skin. Bright red lipstick covered their mouths and various creams and foundations protected the rest of the face. Under different circumstances, it might have been rather funny, but the boys were long past caring about their appearance. They also packed medicine, sunglasses, seat cushions, snowshoes, even the fair child's compass salvaged from the cockpit. Nothing went to waste. Everything that could be used was used. By the second week of December, after 2 months in the mountains, they were ready to go. But there was just enough time for one final tragedy before they departed. Numatici had continued to refuse his meat rations over the previous weeks, and hidden beneath his thick beard and baggy clothing, his body had wasted away to almost nothing. Tokati hadn't been on the old Christian's rugby team, but he had captained a Monte Vido football team called Lyola FC. Before the accident, he'd been an athlete in peak physical condition. But when he died peacefully in his sleep on the 11th of December, 1972, he weighed just 25 kilos. After his death, his friends found a handwritten note clutched in his fist containing a quote from the Bible. Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. Just in case anyone had forgotten their pact, he was giving the others permission to consume what remained of his body. Tokati had been one of the most popular boys in the group and his death hit everyone extremely hard. It also made them all the more determined to end this hell once and for all. Nando Parado took a pair of tiny red shoes from amongst his belongings. He'd bought them in Mendoza what seemed like a lifetime ago as a gift for his baby nephew. One of the shoes he took safely into his pocket, but the other he hung outside the broken fair child. Just before they left, Parado looked each of his friends in the eye and told them he'd be back to pick it up soon. With that, he, Kessa, and Tintin set off on what would be their final expedition. Their mission was simple. Make it back to civilization or die trying. They left camp on December the 12th, 1972. Having ruled out the eastern route on the previous expedition, they once again forged west, straight up the colossal mountain that had towered over them ever since the crash 61 days earlier. More experienced mountaineers, in other words, basically anyone who's ever stepped foot on a mountain, would probably have first hiked north where the slope was less extreme, then followed the ridge of the mountain towards the west. It was longer but much less challenging and a whole lot less dangerous. Instead, Kessa, Parado, and Tintin opted for the shortest route, straight up the steepest part of the mountain. It wasn't entirely new to them. They tackled about half of it on their first major expedition 7 weeks earlier. But even so, the climb proved to be harder than any of them could ever have imagined. The mountains upper slopes were almost comically steep, pushing 60° in places. A fall would have meant certain death. To make matters worse, during the heat of the day, the snow started to melt, soaking into their seat cushion snowshoes and adding several kilos to every step. Their first night in the sleeping bag was, to put it bluntly, terrifying. It wasn't the temperature this time. It was well below freezing, but the bag did its job. No, it was that crazy slope. No seasoned mountaineer would ever attempt to get 40 winks on a 40° slope. Not without physically anchoring themselves to the mountain first. The risk of falling is much too high. The boys didn't know that, of course, but even if they had, they simply didn't have the gear they needed to set up a safe bed for the night. Kanessa would later confess it was the most terrifying night of his entire life, considering what he'd lived through over the previous two months. That's quite the statement. Before setting off, the trio had hoped to complete the climb inside a single day. In reality, it took them free. The final section was the hardest of all, so steep that walking was impossible. Nando Prada led the way, digging hand and footh holes out of the hardpacked snow with a metal pole he' brought along as a walking stick. It took a monumental effort, borderline supernatural given the circumstances, but on the morning of the 15th of December 1972, Nando Parado was the first to make it to the top of that colossal mountain. He had no way of knowing it at the time, but he was the first human being ever to set foot on the summit of this 4,600 m monster. At the time, it didn't even have a name. These days, we know it by the one Nando Parado gave it on that very day. Mount Cellar, named for his father, Cella Parado. Having finally reached the top, the boys were understandably elated, but their joy turned to despair in an instant. Since the crash, the survivors had been working on the assumption that Chile was just a handful of miles away on the other side of this towering peak. On reaching the summit, the boys had fully expected to see green fields and valleys stretching out before them, perhaps even a town or two. Instead, almost as far as the eye could see, there was just more mountains. And that could only mean one thing. They had not, as they had assumed, crashed right on the edge of the Andes. They were lost somewhere smack in the middle. Now, that realization should have broken them. But, and I feel like I've said this already at least a million times in this video, they didn't give up. They took a blow that should have buckled them, and they just got on with it. The most obvious problem they now faced was one of pure logistics. They packed enough food for a hike of about a week. At the time, that felt like a conservative estimate, but it clearly wasn't going to be enough. It left them with a bit of a predicament. well, more of a predicament. Pushing on meant almost certain death by starvation, but going back to camp to supply just wasn't an option either. Scaling the mountain had drained their already dangerously low energy reserves. Doing it all over again would likely kill them. So, what to do? As always, they fought their way out of trouble. They couldn't forge on and they couldn't go back. Instead, they did both. Tintin headed back to the Fairchild on his own, leaving Parado and Kanessa with his share of the food. Things would still be tight, but if they rationed carefully, they might just make it. It had taken them 3 days to reach the summit of the newly named Mount Cellar. But using a seat cushion as a makeshift sled, Tintin made it all the way back to the Fairchild in 45 minutes. It must have been one hell of a ride. Upon the peak, Nando Parado and Roberto Kessa prepared themselves for the final push. From this point on, there would be no going back. It was death or salvation. There was nothing in between. As they stood on the top of that desolate mountain, staring out at the endless sea of snowy peaks, the two young men found themselves holding hands. Before them was a view of both indescribable beauty and utter despair. Kessa turned to Parado with a smile. "You and I are friends," he said. "We've been through so much. Now, let's go die together. Roberto Kessa was 19 at the time, Nando Parado, 23. Neither believed they would ever see their families or friends again. Yet, they just kept on going. Getting down the other side of the mountain was only marginally easier than climbing it had been. The snow was extremely slippery and the going was slow. At one point, Parado tried to speed things up a bit by sliding down a narrow gully on his bum, but within seconds, he was completely out of control. By his own estimations, he hit a top speed of about 60 mph before smashing into a snow drift. After that, they just walked. Before long, they passed the snow line for the first time in almost 2 and 1/2 months. Symbolically, it was a huge moment. But the change of scenery came with a new set of problems. Instead of somewhat predictable snow underfoot, Parado and Kessa had to negotiate huge boulder fields packed with loose and crumbling rocks. Every footstep was a potential death sentence. In their weakened state, a sprained ankle or broken bone from a fall would have probably been game over. There was also a problem with their food. Without the snow to keep things cool, their precious meat began to rot. They were already severely malnourished. If their food became inedible before they found help, they would surely die. Eventually, they made their way down into a huge glacial valley. A mountain stream flowed through the middle, running roughly westwards. So, the boys followed it for mile after punishing mile. It took more than a week of hard hiking before they saw the first tentative signs of human activity. A rusty old ting can. And more encouragingly, a herd of cows. It was proof that other humans had been here, but time was running out. Most of the food was gone, and what remained was rosing. There aren't many things in life more horrific than eating human flesh, I think. But I'm guessing eating rotten human flesh is probably one of them. Both Parado and Kessa were struggling badly. But Kessa in particular had grown alarmingly weak. Every step was a struggle. Every breath a labored wheeze. It was only sheer force of will that kept them moving one day to the next. And then all of a sudden it was over. Well, almost. On the ninth day after leaving camp, Kessa was lying exhausted in the dust when he glanced up and saw three men on horseback staring right at him from the other side of the river. With little else to do, Parado and Kessa settled down to wait and to pray. The following morning, the 10th since they had left camp. They woke to find the horsemen had returned. Seeing that the boys were awake, one of the riders lobbed a large stone across the river. Attached to it was a piece of paper and a pencil. Parado grabbed both and hastily scribbled down a note. This is what it said. I come from an airplane that crashed in the mountains. I am your walking for 10 days. I have a wounded friend up there. In the plane, there are still 14 injured people. We need to get out of here quickly and we don't know how to. We don't have any food. We are very weak. When are you going to come get us? Please. We can't even walk. Where are we? The horse riders had heard all about the missing plane months earlier. It seemed unbelievable that these two emaciated young men could be survivors. But then again, where else could they have come from? This isn't a part of the world where you get many unexpected visitors. And whoever these boys were, it was clear they'd been through hell. The men agreed to help. They sent a rider to pick Parado and Kessa up and take them to a tiny shack where they were given food and water. It's hard to overstate just how close this story came to having a very different ending. The 10-day hike out of the mountains had taken every last ounce of strength Nando Parado and Roberto Canasa possessed. At the time of their rescue, Kessa was essentially paralyzed from exhaustion. Nando would later estimate that his friend was just a single day from death when they were found. Had things played out just a little bit differently, they would have died out there alone in the wilderness, and their friends up in the mountains would never have been found, or at least not alive. Thankfully, things didn't play out differently. Nando and Kessa found help just in time and within 24 hours the Chilean authorities had dispatched three helicopters to find the others. Neither Nando Parado nor Roberto Kanessa could confidently point to the crash site on a map. So despite his newfound and very understandable fear of flying, Nando agreed to guide the helicopters in person. He was able to direct the pilot back through the valleys he'd walked with Kessa without too much trouble and soon they reached the base of Mount Cellar. When Parado gave the next direction straight up, at first the pilot just shook his head. There was no way to emaciated young men with none of the gear and no idea could possibly have come over that mountain, but Parado was insistent and eventually the pilot pulled the helicopter into a steep climb. It was not a smooth journey. The air up there is so thin and the wind's so strong that the pilots physically couldn't get the helicopter over the summit. They had to abort the first attempt altogether and approach the valley from a different angle. Second time around though, they successfully made it over the top. But the change of direction had left Parado a little turned around. The snow-covered valley below was vast and apparently empty. He was just about beginning to doubt himself when he spotted the rock formation he recognized. And shortly after that, the helicopters were circling the Fairchild. I can't even begin to imagine the range of emotions the survivors on the ground must have experienced as the choppers came into land. Even if I could, I'm pretty sure it would be beyond the power of mere words to describe. There were 45 people on board flight 571 when it took off from Mendoza airport bound for Santiago on the 12th of October 1972. Just 16 people were still alive 72 days later when the rescue mission was completed. Those survivors were flown to a hospital in central Santiago. Disbelieving parents began to arrive to see the children most of them had spent the previous weeks mourning. These reunions were moments of pure unfiltered joy. But it was only a matter of time before the survivors would have to talk about exactly what happened up there in the mountains. It was an impossibly difficult situation. Incredible as the rescue had been, the recovery of the survivors wasn't solely cause for celebration. It was also final confirmation that 29 people were dead. That was worldending news. But things got a whole lot harder for the families involved when they discovered their loved ones bodies had been eaten to ensure the survival of the rest. And just as everyone was trying to come to terms with the brutal reality, the newspapers got involved. That 16 people had survived a plane crash and more than two months stranded in the mountains was already big news. But when Chilean newspaper Elmer Curio printed a picture of a halfeaten human leg propped up against the side of the fair child on its front page, it caused a global sensation. A huge public backlash followed. Things got so bad that the survivors were forced to hold a news conference to tell their side of the story. It took place in Monte Vido on December the 28th, just 5 days after the rescue. At first, the survivors weren't sure how to breach the subject. Some people wanted to talk frankly about what had happened. Others wanted to gloss over some of the gorier details. In the end, they opted for simple honesty. The decision could easily have backfired, but the response was overwhelmingly positive. The news conference ended with a standing ovation from the assembled journalists. And not long afterwards, Pope John Paul V 6 sent a telegram absolving the survivors of any guilt for their actions. Perhaps the most amazing reaction of all came from the parents of the children who didn't make it out of the mountains. Despite everything that had happened, almost without exception, they were united in their support of the survivors. Several went so far as to express their gratitude that even in death, their children had helped to ensure the survival of the rest. It's more than 50 years since Flight 571 was lost in the Andes. Each year on December the 22nd, the survivors of that terrible tragedy get together to mark the anniversary of their rescue. Nando Parado describes a date as their shared birthday, the day each of them was reborn against all Leons. I've covered hundreds of stories on this channel over the years. Many have featured humanity at its very worst. The Miracle of the Andes is a shining example of us at our best. It's a story of resilience, belief, friendship, and determination. More than anything, it's a story of sheer indomitable will. I truly hope you enjoyed it and thanks for watching.

It's always been rare, and there's a good chance it always will be rare. And because of this, the price of gold has always increased over time. There have been short-term fluctuations, but you can pretty much count on the price of gold increasing far into the future. And because of this, nations know that if their fiat-based economy takes a dive, if say a black swan event happens and the S&P 500 drops 20 percentage points over 24 hours, then having a large national gold reserve is invaluable. And it isn't like gold is exclusively used during catastrophic events. Gold reserves are used on a regular basis to hedge against inflation. Whereas fiat currencies can be endlessly printed and the supply can balloon within days, the supply of gold typically increases by just 2% per year because it's rare, time consuming, and costly to mine. So during recessions, private investors usually turn to buying up more gold as a safety net. And central banks are no different. A nation having strong gold reserves in the modern day also has another notable benefit. It increases that country's perceived trust. Pretend for a moment you are Japan, a country which lends money to a lot of other nations. And imagine that the United Kingdom, for example, comes knocking at your door and says, "Hi, Japan. We're a bit broke at the moment and we've pissed all of our taxpayers money up the wall, so we'd like to borrow 1 billion from you." Japan says, "No problem at all, but we're going to charge you 2% interest, so you need to pay us20 million per year." £20 million a year is a hefty sum. And if the British economy hits a rough patch, which is basically the status quo in Britain, they may not have sufficient funds in the Treasury to make their interest payments to Japan on time. Well, not to worry because they can always dip into their gold reserves to settle the bill. Of course, Japan already knows that the UK has a handsome 16 billion pounds of gold reserves. So, Japan's confidence in the UK's ability to pay their interest is very high, which gives countries like the UK, US, Germany, Italy, and many other developed nations with massive gold reserves the freedom to go on freewheeling borrowing sprees and hoover up sovereign loans like sweets at a pick a mix. Today, all of the G7 holds vast gold reserves for the reasons we've discussed, except for one country. What if I said that one of these major nations has zero gold reserves? Can you guess which it is? It's Canada. Since 1965, Canada has been steadily selling its national gold reserves. Their finance ministry argued that in a world where currencies are no longer backed by gold, there is no point in holding any of it. Today, they have no official gold reserves, apart from a few measly coins here and there, which very much makes them an outlier. Instead, Canada has invested heavily into financial markets, which is an interesting play. The potential for growth there is much higher, but it's also a lot riskier. As we've discussed, a market crash could wipe tens or even hundreds of billions off their GDP. So far, it's worked out okay for them. Canada has a pretty stable economy. Maple syrup just tastes too damn good. But time will tell if going cold turkey on gold was incredibly brave or incredibly stupid. Today, there is a lot of talk about America's huge gold reserves in Fort Knox. There are conspiracies that it might not all be there. Most likely it is, but if it is externally audited, we will know sooner or later. However, I want to leave you with an interesting fact about how a large amount of that gold made it into Fort Knox in the first place. It may surprise you to know that it was stolen from Americans themselves. In 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102, which made it illegal for US citizens to physically own gold coins and gold bullions within the United States. The logic was that citizens hoarding gold was leading to market stagnation. So, it was meant to revitalize the economy at a very difficult time. During this time, Americans had to hand over all of their private gold reserves or face up to 10 years in prison. Millions of dollars worth of gold was confiscated with people being compensated at below market rates. Most of it was scirled away in Fort Knox and added to the national gold reserves. So whether or not national gold reserves remain a sensible idea even today, I think we can all agree that pretty much all of them have been accumulated through highly questionable means. And on that depressing note, thanks for watching.

and self-sufficiency to a huge   force of unprecedentedly mobile 
and extremely deadly fighters   and you had an incredibly lethal combination. And the rest of the world 
simply wasn't ready for it. Speaking of the rest of the world, with 
all of the Mongolian Steppe now under   his command, Genghis Khan turned 
his attention to the lands beyond. First up on the Mongol menu was the Chinese 
imperial dynasty of Western Xia, a key part   of the Silk Road and, more importantly, 
an entry point into the rest of China. To an outside observer Genghis Khan's invasion 
of Western Xia would probably have looked like   a huge tactical blunder. For one thing 
the Mongols were outnumbered two to one,   but there was also the small matter of the entire 
Gobi desert that lay between them and the enemy. The idea of a giant army crossing the 
world's sixth largest desert with 30,000   men on horses might sound insane, but while 
the Mongols weren't exactly desert people,   they were incredibly hardy. When times got 
especially tough, they would drink milk from   their horses in order to stay alive. And when 
times got *oh-shit-we're-all-going-to-die* tough,   they would open a vein on their 
horses' flank and drink the blood. So, thanks to a spot of equine vampirism 
the Mongol horde made it safely across   the desert. But what they found on 
the other side was just as daunting. The tribes of the Mongolian Steppe were 
nomadic - they moved their camps around   with the seasons to ensure a constant 
supply of food both for themselves and   for their livestock - especially the horses. 
But by their very nature nomadic tribes don't   tend to be overly big on building things. So 
when Genghis Khan turned up in Western Xia   spoiling for a fight, he was faced with 
something he'd never seen before: walls. OK so Genghis Khan probably knew what 
walls were, but the fact remained that,   being a nomad, he didn't have all that much 
experience with them. And that was a problem,   because in Western Xia they were 
absolutely bloody everywhere. When the Great Khan's mighty horde arrived 
outside the thick walls of the capital of   Zhongxing in 1209, it was clear that 
an attack was impossible. Instead,   the Mongols were forced to camp 
outside while their mightiest military   minds tried to figure out just what 
the hell they were going to do next. Destroying the walls wasn't an option because the 
Mongols had never developed any siege weapons (not   that you can really blame them - you don't 
exactly need a trebuchet to break into a   yurt). After double-checking that horses 
definitely couldn't climb walls - worth a   try - one of the Khan's commanders came up with 
an intriguing (and absolutely brutal) idea - if   they couldn't break through the walls, why 
not just murder everyone inside instead? To that end the Mongols started building a large 
dam across the mighty Yellow River that flowed   alongside the city. The plan was simple: change 
the course of the river so that it ran smack   through the middle of Zhongxing, drowning every 
man, woman, and child inside in the process. Luckily for the people of Zhongxing, the 
tent-dwelling Mongols weren't exactly the world's   greatest builders, and while they *did* succeed 
in diverting the river, rather than engulf the   city as intended they managed to flood their own 
camp instead. Not Genghis Khan's finest hour that. Still, in the end it was only a minor 
setback. Despite having far more soldiers,   the Western Xia army was poorly led and 
scattered across the country, with the   bulk of the men far away on the southern border. 
They were simply no match for the mighty Mongol   murder machine, and after suffering a series 
of defeats, in 1210 Western Xia surrendered,   effectively becoming the first vassal 
state of the world's newest empire. Genghis Khan wasted no time pushing deeper 
into China and the territory of the powerful   Jin dynasty. As we've already seen, it's 
likely he'd spent some time as a slave   under the Jin emperors after his defeat at the 
hands of Jamukha. If that was indeed the case,   the time had come to take his revenge. 
And you know what they say - revenge   is a dish best served by 75,000 men on 
horseback murdering everyone in sight. If invading Western Xia had been a bold move, 
taking on the Jin Dynasty was practically   suicidal - by some counts, the Mongol army 
was outnumbered *eight-to-one* by their Jin   counterparts. Not only that, but Jin territory 
was defended by the legendary Great Wall of China,   although luckily for the Mongols, in those days it 
was more of a 'fairly decent palisade' of China,   and in the end they made it into Jin 
territory without too much trouble. As had been the case in Western Xia, 
the Mongols still had to figure out how   the hell to attack all those cities with 
great big walls that were inconveniently   dotted around everywhere - including the 
Jin capital Zhongdu, modern day Beijing. But this is where the brilliance of Genghis Khan's 
meritocracy really started to pay dividends.   Because it was largely son-of-a-blacksmith-Subutai 
who figured out what to do next. He realised that it was ultimately pointless 
for the Mongol army to attack the larger Jin   cities without siege weapons - it would take 
too long and cost too many lives. Instead,   he suggested they should do the exact 
opposite and attack... everything else. Guided by Subutai, the Mongol army 
went on an absolute rampage, tearing   across Jin lands and annihilating absolutely 
everything that wasn't protected by a wall.   They burned fields and razed villages. They 
murdered tens of thousands of peasants and   took tens of thousands more prisoner to use 
as human shields against Jin soldiers. When   they came to larger towns they would attack 
with lightning speed, capture the settlement,   then immediately retreat, forcing the Jin to 
spend time and energy reoccupying strategically   unimportant territory. For the Jin it was like 
fighting smoke. Really fucking angry smoke. The net result was utter chaos, and refugees 
soon clogged the streets as food supplies   dwindled. Suddenly being ensconced behind high 
city walls didn’t feel quite so safe anymore. At the same time, Genghis Khan was learning. 
Sooner or later he was going to have to figure   out how to take large cities, and that 
meant developing siege weapons. Since   none of his men had any idea how to do that, 
he instead began covertly recruiting siege   engineers directly from the enemy. 
Soon enough Jin siege experts were   teaching the Mongols how to build catapults 
to break down the walls of their own cities. This willingness to learn from the 
people he conquered would become a   defining trait of Genghis Khan's Empire. 
As well as siege weapons the Mongols   gained written language from the Uighurs 
and gunpowder weapons from the Chinese,   along with a whole host of armour and weapon 
upgrades from the various people they conquered. Despite Subutai's war of chaos in the countryside 
and the Mongol's ever-improving skills in siege   warfare, Genghis Khan was unable to completely 
defeat the Jin, and in 1215 he returned to the   Mongolian Steppe. With China proving a 
tough nut to crack for the time being,   he instead began to look to the west 
to the empire of the Qara Khitai. A few years earlier in 1213 the Qara Khitai 
dynasty had been overthrown in a coup staged   by a chap called Kuchlug. As it happens, Kuchlug 
was a (former) prince of the Mongolian Steppe   who'd been forced to flee west when Genghis 
Khan defeated his tribe. Kuchlug had wasted   no time making his mark on his new empire, and 
in 1216 he attempted to expand it by attacking   the nearby city of Almaliq. This turned out to 
be a monumentally terrible idea for two reasons. One, Almaliq was under the governorship of the 
Karluks, vassals of the Mongolian Empire. And two,   the city was ruled by Genghis Khan's 
grandson-in-law - and if there was   one thing you really, *really* didn't want to 
be doing in 13th century Central Asia it was   murdering members of Genghis Khan's extended 
family... as Kuchlug was about to find out. The Great Khan promptly dispatched 20,000 warriors 
to liberate Almaliq and hunt down Kuchlug. As   per usual the Mongols were outnumbered, but - 
also as per usual - it didn't matter. Kuchlug   suffered several heavy defeats, and soon enough 
entire cities were defecting to the Mongols,   although for once it had nothing to do 
with their fear of imminent destruction. You see, Kuchlug was a Buddhist, and after gaining 
power he'd begun ruthlessly persecuting the local   muslims. Genghis Khan, on the other hand, had 
realised early on that religious persecution would   only cause him a headache he didn't need. Instead, 
he allowed free practice of any and all religions   within his growing empire. Bearing in mind that 
freedom of religion isn't exactly a given in   many parts of the world even today, it's fair to 
say this policy was centuries ahead of its time. Between the military victories and countless 
defections, the Mongols polished off the vast   Qara Khitai empire in under a year, 
giving Genghis Khan huge swathes of   land across modern day China, Kazakhstan, 
Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. By this point I assume the world's cartographers 
had all gone on strike citing impossible working   conditions - thanks to the Mongol's ceaseless 
victories the world's borders were changing   on an almost weekly basis. And after 
the assimilation of the Qara Khitai   empire by the Mongol Borg, one of those 
brand-spanking new borders now lay between   two of the world's great superpowers 
- the Mongol and Khwarazmian Empires. After a solid 30 years or so of almost 
non-stop war, Genghis Khan had apparently   had enough of fighting, because for once 
he didn't go to meet his new neighbours   all-bows-blazing. The Khwarazmian Empire was a 
wealthy centre of culture and learning that lay   along an important section of the Silk Road. 
So rather than attempt yet another invasion,   Genghis Khan decided to try and make 
friends with the empire's powerful Shah. In 1218 he sent a grand caravan of some 450 
merchants carrying steel, silk, and other   valuables to establish a trade route between the 
two empires. When the merchants arrived in the   city of Otrar, the local governor was absolutely 
delighted with the riches he saw before him. So   delighted, in fact, that he decided to simply take 
them for himself and murder all the merchants that   had brought them. (Spoiler alert, things aren't 
going to end well for the greedy governor). Genghis Khan was on the other side of Asia 
at the time, fighting his old foes the Jin.   But when he heard what had happened 
to his trade caravan he immediately   dispatched a diplomatic envoy directly 
to the Shah to demand an explanation. Now, I can only assume the Khwarazmian top brass 
hadn't been watching CNN over the previous 10   years or so, because it seems they had absolutely 
no idea just who the fuck they were dealing with. Rather than do the sensible thing and get 
down on his hands and knees to beg for mercy,   the Shah only bloody went and doubled down by 
murdering - or in some cases mutilating - the   Mongolian diplomats. (Spoiler alert, things 
aren't going to end well for him either). As you can probably imagine, when our 
friend Genghis heard about this latest   insult... he absolutely lost his shit. 
Despite being in the middle of a mini   war in Jin territory he essentially 
just downed tools and rode west. Genghis Khan had shown himself to 
be incredibly ruthless during his   years uniting the tribes and the wars 
of expansion that followed. But his   campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire was 
something new. This wasn't about expansion,   it was about revenge. The Mongol horde 
devastated the Khwarazmian Empire in   what remains to this day one of the bloodiest 
military campaigns in all of human history. Genghis divided his army into 5 separate forces 
that operated independently, appearing as if   from nowhere and striking with lightning speed. 
Any cities that resisted the Mongol Horde - and   several did - were utterly annihilated. In 
some cases, entire populations were slaughtered   to a man, and by some estimates a total of 15 
million people were killed during the campaign. In just two years, the black hole 
that was the Mongolian empire had   devoured another meal - and grown correspondingly. Oh, and if you're wondering what happened to our 
friends the governor of Otrar and the Shah of the   empire, allow me to tell you. The man who kicked 
this whole crazy business off by murdering the   Mongolian Merchants was captured by the Khan's 
men and executed. But there would be no swift   beheading in his case. No, as punishment for 
his greed in stealing the Mongolian trade goods,   the governor was put to death through 
the unimaginably painful process of   having molten silver poured into his eyes, 
ears, and mouth. Yeeeah that’ll do it. As for the Shah, he went into full retreat, 
fleeing from the advancing Mongols as if all   the devils of the seventh circle of 
hell were hot on his heels. Which I   suppose from his perspective they basically 
were. It's thought that he made it as far   as the Caspian sea where he died shitting 
himself - no seriously, he had dysentery. With another remarkable victory under his 
belt Genghis Khan headed back east to China,   where a rebellion was in full swing in the lands 
of Western Xia. But by now he was an old man,   and, somewhat unexpectedly, his prodigious 
strength was finally about to fail him. Exactly what it was that killed Genghis Khan 
remains unknown to this day. Considering how   much war he'd waged in his 6-and-a-bit decades on 
God's green earth it would have been fitting for   him to have died in battle, but no. Up until 
relatively recently it was generally believed   he fell ill after being thrown from his horse 
during a hunt. But more recently scholars have   speculated that he may actually have died from 
bubonic plague. (Incidentally, it's thought to   have been the Mongols that brought the Black Death 
to Europe during the siege of Caffa as part of one   of the world's earliest examples of biological 
warfare… but that's a story for another day.). Whatever it was that killed him, in 1227 Genghis 
Khan was no more. But not even the death of its   founder could stop the Juggernaut that was the 
Mongol Empire - Genghis Khan's descendents would   continue to build on his work for the following 
140 years. At its peak, the Empire would cover   more than 9 million square miles - that’s almost 
two and a half times the size of Europe - and   contain more than 100 million people, about 
25% of the world’s population at the time. The Mongol Empire remains to this day the largest 
contiguous - or ‘interconnected’ - empire in   history, and the second largest overall behind 
the British Empire of the early 20th century. Genghis Khan died almost eight hundred 
years ago, but it seems that eight centuries   haven't quite been enough for the world 
to figure out exactly what to make of him. He’s often been portrayed - especially in the 
west - as a ruthless and bloodthirsty warlord   intent on conquering the world by any means 
necessary. But every villain is a hero to someone,   and it turns out there are really quite 
a lot of someones who see Genghis Khan   as a truly revolutionary leader whose brutal 
methods were simply a product of their time. As is usually the case, the truth is probably a   shade of grey that lies somewhere in 
between those two black and whites. There's no denying that he was one of the 
most charismatic and successful leaders in   history. That he achieved everything 
he did after being abandoned by his   tribe at the age of 8 is genuinely almost 
unbelievable. By all logic he should have   starved to death on the Mongolian Steppe 
before he even reached adulthood. And yet   somehow he not only survived - he went on to 
found one of the largest empires in history. Not only that, as well as all the conquering 
stuff he also encouraged international trade,   promoted the spread of ideas across the world, 
supported freedom of religion, revolutionised   warfare, and built a genuine meritocracy 
that celebrated ability, not birthright. Of course, there's *also* no denying that Genghis 
Khan was incredibly brutal when he needed to be…   and probably sometimes simply when he wanted 
to be too. He believed in utterly destroying   his enemies so as to ensure they would 
never pose a threat in the future, and he   was prepared to follow through on that belief 
by... basically murdering everyone in sight. Ultimately, it's difficult to judge 
the deeds of a man who lived 800   years ago - by modern standards he was a 
genocidal land-grabbing maniac. But then   again, so was everyone else you 
learned about in history class. Whatever your views on the man, the myth, the 
legend, what isn't up for debate is that Genghis   Khan was one of the most influential human 
beings ever to have lived. A force of nature   who dramatically changed our world in 
ways that are still being felt today. Thanks for watching.
